issue_context.title: Assertion failure in the QUIC TXP
issue_context.body:
Running the test added in #21368 results in the following assertion failure:

````
ssl/quic/quic_txp.c:2218: OpenSSL internal error: Assertion failed: h.bytes_appended > 0
````
comments:
As I suspected, this is due to a mismatch in the criteria for the functions to determine if a packet should be generated (pending) and the functions to actually generate a packet. A packet with a zero-length payload is not allowed in QUIC. We expect our pending function to be completely accurate here.

The specific problem is that congestion control is limiting the size of the packet generated to 24 bytes (which is fine) which leads to a maximum payload size of 3 bytes. The TXP wants to generate an ACK frame, but there is not enough room to encode one.

Fix might be a bit awkward; thinking about it.
Doesn't QUIC have a 1200 minimum packet size?

> Doesn't QUIC have a 1200 minimum packet size?

To be specific, QUIC requires that a network path be able to support a maximum UDP datagram payload size of 1200 bytes. A QUIC datagram can contain multiple QUIC packets in the same datagram, so a single QUIC packet may need to be constructed to a budget of less than 1200 bytes if a packet has already been placed in the datagram, partially consuming the 1200 byte budget for that datagram. A budget of less than 1200 bytes could also occur due to limits imposed by the congestion controller.

review_comments: As a (future) optimization it would probably make sense in future to record the minimum enc level at which we actually can send packets because all the lower levels have been discarded already and start with that one.
I thought we had this information already?

It is worth noting that the first test in the enc_level loop is a call to `txp_should_try_staging` which tests `ossl_qtx_is_enc_level_provisioned` first. So unprovisioned (e.g. dropped) ELs are rejected very quickly. I doubt this would make a measurable performance difference.

Does this check that the HANDSHAKE packet is generated actually - at least when it fits? If I understand this right if TXP just padded the INITIAL packet instead of bothering generating the handshake packet even if it fits, it would still pass?
Good point. I will raise a small extra test as as a separate PR after this merges.
